To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

codelivery of DNA plasmids coding for CD86 and the glycoprotein of herpes simplex virus or the ovalbumin results in the down-modulation of the immune responses to the plasmids coding these antigens, with a stronger effect on cell-mediated immune responses.

the codelivery of plasmid DNA coding for the extracellulare domains of CD86 is able to down-regulate the immune response to plasmid DNA encoding for a soluble protein and for a membrane-bound protein, and that this effect could be due to the preferential engagement of the soluble form of the CD86 to CTLA4.
the codelivery of plasmids encoding for the extracellullar domain of CD86 along DNA vaccines results in the downregulation of the cell-mediated and humoral immune response.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach to the inhibition of the immune response by codelivery with a DNA vaccine of a plasmids encoding for the soluble form (DeltaCD86) of a costimulatory molecule.
the development of a strategy to modulate the immune response by the use of a plasmids coding for the extracelular domains of CD86.
the development of new strategies for the down-modulation of the immune system in order to prevent or treat autoimmune diseases and to avoid or reduce the side effects of DNA vaccines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the coadministration of a plasmids encoding for the extracelullar domains of CD86 and a plasmids coding for a membrane-bound or a soluble protein by the im route resulted in a down-regulation of both humoral and cellular immune responses to DNA vaccines in the spleen, and a strong inhibition of cell-mediated immune response to DNA vaccination in the draining lymph nodes.
pDelta86 can be a useful tool to inhibit DNA vaccines, and the inhibition is dependent on the nature of the antigen and its localization.
the codelivery of DeltaCD86 with a DNA vaccine results in the down-modulation of both humoral and cellular immune responses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
codelivery of DNA vaccines coding for soluble costimulatory molecules could be a useful strategy for down-regulation of T cell-mediated immunity.

the down-regulation observed in the humoral immune responses could be explained by the fact that DeltaCD86 binds CTLA-4 and CD28, whereas the down-regulation in the cell-mediated immune responses could be due to the engagement of DeltaCD8 to CTLA-1 but not to CD28, which could lead to the inhibition of the activation of T cells.
the codelivery of DNA encoding for the extracelluar domains of CD86 and the DNA coding for the protein of interest can be an effective strategy to down-regulate the immune response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the codelivery of DNA encoding for the extracellullar domains of CD86 results into a strong inhibition of DNA vaccine immunogenicity.
it is possible to down-regulate the immune response to a DNA vaccine by the coadministration of a DNA coding for a costimulatory molecule.
the codelivery of plasmid DNA coding for the extracelullar domains of CD86 is able to down-regulate the immune response in vivo to plasmid DNA encoding for a membrane-bound or for a soluble protein.
